The material facts of the case as emerged from the DAR are that on 01.03.2021 at about 08:00 a.m., the petitioner Sameer Singh, aged 15 years, along with his friend, after performing running in District Park, Nand Nagri, was returning home and while he was crossing the road at Char Khamba Red Light Intersection, Nand Nagri, Delhi, an Alto Car bearing no. DL6CR-2555 (hereinafter referred to as "offending vehicle"), being driven by respondent no.1 Ankit Sagar at a high speed,
rashly and negligently, hit the petitioner from behind.
As a result, the petitioner fell down on the road and the rear tyre of a bus that was crossing the intersection, went over his legs.

sentences.text: I heard the final arguments advanced by learned counsels for the parties and also perused the evidence and other materials placed on record.

My findings on the issues are as under:-
ISSUE NO.1

Whether petitioner suffered injuries during the accident occurred on 01.03.2021 at about 09:30 p.m., near Char Khamba Red Light, Nand Nagri, within the jurisdiction of PS Nand Nagri, due to rash and negligent driving of the vehicle bearing no. DL6CR-2555, being driven by respondent no.1/ driver? OPP 11.
It is settled proposition of law that, in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine-qua-non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of the preponderance of probabilities.
A holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

ISSUE NO.2 Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom?
OPP COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION 23.
Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be a pittance.

"Just compensation" cannot be equated with bonanza but it suggests application of fair and equitable principles and reasonable approach of the Tribunal while awarding t h e c o m p e n s a t i o n . sentences.text: 24. The present claim petition pertains to injury and scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.

sentences.text:
The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking, while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial; (iii) other material losses.

So far non-pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e., on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii)
damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal Dar - Master Samir vs Ankit Sagar And Ors on 10 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/130952478/

sentences.text: Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.

entities.text: Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:
"4.

The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act," for short) make it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of Treatment.
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
(iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

OPP 3. Relief.
A man is not compensated for the physical injury which he might have received in the accident caused by the motor vehicle in a public place, rather he is compensated for the loss, which he suffered as a result of that injury that he suffered in the accident.
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of Treatment.
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
(iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is settled proposition of law that, in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine-qua-non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of the preponderance of probabilities.
A holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
17. On perusal of FIR, which is part of the DAR, it is clear that the accident occurred 01.03.2021 and the FIR was registered on the same day and the registration number of offending vehicle is found clearly mentioned in the FIR and the offending vehicle was taken into police possession from the spot of the accident itself.
Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be a pittance.
"Just compensation" cannot be equated with bonanza but it suggests application of fair and equitable principles and reasonable approach of the Tribunal while awarding t h e c o m p e n s a t i o n . 24. The present claim petition pertains to injury and scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.
The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act," for short) make it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
Therefore, being a student, the petitioner is not entitled to any loss of income during treatment.
The disablement and loss of earning capacity are two different aspects and not Dar - Master Samir vs Ankit Sagar And Ors on 10 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/130952478/
8 substitute for each other and the loss of income has to be seen considering the profession in which the petitioner was engaged at the time of the accident.
In this case, the petitioner has not examined the concerned doctor to bring on record as to what physical restrictions the petitioner would face with 3% permanent disability and further, no evidence has been brought on record to indicate that with such disability, the petitioner would face any loss of future income.
The extent of disability being so minimal, this Tribunal is not convinced that that would create any hindrance to the earning capacity of the petitioner and therefore, no compensation is granted to the petitioner under this head.
Thus, considering the nature of injury and the period of treatment, an inference can be drawn that the petitioner had to spend a reasonable amount on high and rich protein diet for the purpose of early recovery, post-surgery and for visiting the hospital/ doctor during treatment.
Considering the nature of injury and period of treatment as discussed above under the head of "special diet and conveyance charges", it may be safely inferred that the treatment of the petitioner would have continued for about five months and therefore, the father of the minor injured is required to be granted attendant charges to compensate loss of his earnings for five months on account of providing assistance to/ attending his injured son in his routine activities and taking care of him during treatment period (Refer : DTC & Ors Vs. Lalita, 1983 ACJ 253).

Thus, it is clear that due to the injuries sustained in the accident, the petitioner/ injured must have gone through immense pain and suffering during his treatment and, therefore, a sum of Rs.50,000/- is awarded to the petitioner under this head.
